newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe in confidence crisis - Schmidhuber.
newsitem.headline: Europe in confidence crisis - Schmidhuber.

text.p: European integration has entered a crisis of confidence, with a resurgence of national interests souring public opinion and making the European currency unpopular, a senior Bundesbank official said.
Bundesbank board member Peter Schmidhuber said on Friday that political and psychological problems now posed a greater obstacle to monetary union than economic conditions.

"Despite official statements to the contrary, we are facing a crisis of confidence in European integration," he told a forum on European monetary union in Otzenhausen, Germany. "It is currently focused on the 'unpopular euro'."

He warned that criticism of the German position on EMU -- particularly from France, but also from other countries -- ran the risk of burdening the relationship between Germany and these countries if the attacks persisted.

Schmidhuber blamed growing political doubts about the basic tenets of European integration -- such as the transfer of sovereignty on certain issues to supranational bodies -- for growing public uncertainty and confusion about the project.
"There has been a slide back into nationalistic thinking," Schmidhuber, a former European commissioner, said according to the text of a speech released in advance of delivery.
"This unfortunately leads me to conclude that the political-psychological bases for the introduction of a common currency are worse than the economic prerequisites," he said.

In his speech, entitled "European Economic and Monetary Union -- a German project?", Schmidhuber argued forcefully that EMU was neither a German, a French, nor an Italian project, but a joint European bid to find a global survival strategy.

Although some elements of the project, notably the parts of the Maastricht Treaty which called for stability policies within monetary union, were in line with German wishes, Bonn had been forced into compromise on other areas, he noted.
"Germany's primary goal in the negotiations on the Treaty was the creation of a political union in the form of a federal European state," he said.
"We only made a small amount of headway on this, not least due to the opposition of the United Kingdom," he added.
Although the inter-governmental conference now taking place was intended to make progress toward political union, there was little hope that much real progress would be made.

"The course of this conference so far...does not justify great hopes that a material deepening of the EU could succeed," he said. "This is a game which in the best case has not been lost. It is much more likely that a few cosmetic additions will be agreed to avoid the fiasco of a public failure," he added.

Even in areas where Germany had got its way, such as on the question of monetary stability, the joint position agreed was "not a German special request, but the a policy which lies in the common interest of all member states," Schmidhuber said.

Turning to the question of attacks on the German position from other European Union states, Schmidhuber pointed to the constant calls from others for Germany to lower interest rates to give relief to other European currencies.
"This is the reason why there are always constant hints that the Bundesbank should loosen its policy, an easing which would not be justified by the domestic situation in Germany," he said.

He also attacked proposals from France to set up a political counterweight to the independent European Central Bank, saying that this idea was not supported by the Maastricht Treaty, which maps out the framework and conditions for EMU.
"The question has to be asked as to how seriously our partners are taking the ECB's independence, apart from accepting the legal texts," he said.
